reason: Flower buds can be hairy, and the examples are correct.
A corona can be short, and 'shorter than' is a comparison of length.
Corona, its lobes and its scales can be minute or small.
The rostellum (orchid) has a colour, such as white or pale yellow.
A perianth tube or basal swelling can be ellipsoid, and ellipsoid is mapped to prolate.
A glume can be firm. This is a texture term for glume consistency.
An anther cap has a 2-D shape such as ovate or triangular.
A disk, ridge or callus can be warty (verrucose).
A lip or lobule can be semiorbicular, which is semicircular.
A leaf sheath auricle can be short.
A fruit (utricle) can have a ciliate margin. The examples say the margins are ciliate, so the reading is a bit indirect, with only one flora.
A utricle surface can be punctate (dotted).
A nutlet can be chestnut or castaneous, which is red-brown.
A glume can be castaneous or chestnut-brown, which is red-brown.
The examples read 'orifice entire', so 'entire' describes the orifice margin and not the fruit. This is the wrong part.
A utricle can be ellipsoid, and ellipsoid is mapped to prolate.
A funicle can be thick, in English and in French (épais).
Parts can be fused or joined, and the examples are correct.
A base or tube can be inflated.
A mesochile (orchid lip part) can be short.
A leaf tooth can have a retuse apex.
The examples are about being sessile, pedunculate or racemose-like. PATO 'structure' is far too generic, and a rule or a more specific term should be used instead.
A leaf tip can be filiform.
A surface part can be wrinkled.
A stipule or its base can be hastate.
Leaf lobes can overlap.
A leaflet can be trifid or tripartite.
A stylopodium can be raised.
The examples mix 'exceeding' and 'long' with plain measurements such as '4-8 mm long'. A rule would need to separate measured values from a qualitative 'long' or 'exceeding'.
'Irregular' means zygomorphic or uneven in a petal, and a petal margin that is irregular is a different thing. A rule would need to tell shape irregularity from margin and pattern irregularity.
Parts can be fleshy (charnu).
'Dark' is a colour darkness, and the examples also describe dark spots, an eye or a throat, which are patterns on parts of the corolla. A rule would need to tell the whole corolla from its marks.
A staminode can be keeled or carinate.
A standard (banner petal) can be reflexed.
A thorn can be persistent, which is non-deciduous.
A disk can be shallow.
An epichile can be triangular or deltoid.
The examples say 'armed with stinging hairs', which is indumentum (hairs). PATO 'disposition' is a wrong reading.
A flower can be ciliate, although in some examples the margin of a flower part is meant.
Parts can be curved or incurved.
A petal apex can be reflexed.
The examples say 'margin dentate at base', so the leaf base only locates the toothed margin. A rule would need to map 'margin ... at base' to the leaf margin.
A hyaline ligule is translucent, so transparent fits.
Glumes can be open or gaping.
An epichile margin can be crenulate, which is scalloped.
Parts can be incurved (incurvé), which is curved.
A scale leaf can be glabrous.
A leaf lobe can be ovate. Ovoid for a flat lobe is read as ovate.
'Attenuated' is a leaf shape (tapering). PATO_0002147 is 'reduced virulence', so this is a wrong reading.
A crown can be wide.
'Entre-noeuds courts' means short internodes, not short nodes. A rule would need to send internodes to the internode part.
A bracteole base can be dilated or expanded.
The examples say 'lobes recurved' and 'recurved at apex'. These probably belong to the stigma or style lobes and not the ovary itself.
A nectary can project (protrude).
An epichile can be hairy.
The examples are 'acute' or 'apiculate' apex and angle, which are shapes. A rule would need to map acute and apiculate to apex shape terms instead of sharpness.
A mid-lobe can be ligulate, which is strap-shaped.
Style branches can be recurved.
A leaf lamina can be fragile.
A perianth or limb can be ellipsoid, and ellipsoid is mapped to prolate.
